name: Infrastructure as Code
description: Provision and manage cloud infrastructure declaratively and repeatably.

topics.name: Terraform
topics.summary: HashiCorp's declarative IaC tool for provisioning infrastructure across AWS, Azure, GCP and more.

lessons.title: What is Terraform and why IaC?
lessons.content:
## The idea

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means describing servers, networks and databases in versioned files instead of clicking in a console.

## How Terraform works

**Terraform** reads `.tf` files written in HCL, compares them with the real world, and makes a plan to reconcile the two.

## Key ideas

- **Providers** talk to APIs (aws, azurerm, google, kubernetes...)
- **Resources** are the things you create
- **State** records what Terraform manages
- **Plan / Apply** previews changes, then executes them

## Try it

Install it from the HashiCorp website and check the version:

```bash
terraform -version
```

## Practice

**Practice:** Install Terraform and run `terraform -help`.

lessons.title: Your first configuration
Variables, outputs and locals
Remote state and backends
lessons.content:
## Remote state and locking

Local state breaks as soon as a team shares infrastructure. Store it remotely with locking:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "my-tf-state"
    key            = "prod/network.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
```

Equivalent backends exist for Azure (`azurerm` storage account) and GCP (`gcs` bucket).

## Commands and safety

Useful commands: `terraform state list`, `terraform import`, `terraform state mv`.

Never commit state files: they can contain secrets.

lessons.title: Modules and team workflows
lessons.content:
## Modules and a team workflow

A **module** is a folder of `.tf` files you call with inputs:

```hcl
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "5.8.1"
  name    = "main"
  cidr    = "10.0.0.0/16"
}
```

## Production workflow

Production workflow:

1. `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate` in CI
2. Post `terraform plan` output on pull requests
3. Apply only from the main branch
4. Scan with `tflint` / `checkov`

The Terraform Registry publishes working AWS, Azure and GCP modules you can study.

description: From virtual machines to containers to orchestrating them at scale.

topics.name: Virtual Machines
topics.summary: Understand hypervisors, VM images, networking and when VMs still beat containers.

lessons.title: How virtualization works
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Basic operating system ideas (processes, the kernel, memory) and a Linux command line.

## What you will learn
How a hypervisor runs several full operating systems on one physical machine, the difference between type 1 and type 2 hypervisors, and what that design costs you.

## What a hypervisor does
A **hypervisor** gives each virtual machine (VM) its own virtual CPUs, memory, disks and network cards.

Modern CPUs make this fast. Intel VT-x and AMD-V let guest code run directly on the processor. When the guest tries a privileged operation, such as changing page tables or talking to a device, the CPU traps to the hypervisor, which handles it and resumes the guest. Second-level address translation (Intel EPT, AMD NPT) maps guest memory to host memory in hardware. For devices, guests use paravirtualized drivers such as **virtio**, which are much faster than emulating a real network card.

To the host, each virtual CPU is usually just a thread. That is why a provider can sell a "2 vCPU" VM on a 96-core server.

## Type 1 and type 2
- **Type 1 (bare metal):** the hypervisor runs directly on the hardware. Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, and KVM, a Linux kernel module that turns Linux itself into a hypervisor. AWS Nitro is based on KVM.
- **Type 2 (hosted):** the hypervisor is an application on a normal desktop OS. Examples: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

Clouds and data centres use type 1. Type 2 is for laptops and testing.

## What the design costs
Every VM boots its own kernel. That gives strong isolation, because a crash or kernel bug inside one guest stays inside it. The price is overhead: a VM usually takes tens of seconds to boot, and each guest OS holds hundreds of megabytes of memory before your application starts. Containers, covered in the Docker topic, share one kernel and avoid that cost, with weaker isolation.

## Worked example
On a Linux machine, check whether the CPU supports virtualization and whether you are already inside a VM.

```bash
grep -E -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo   # vmx = Intel, svm = AMD
lsmod | grep kvm
systemd-detect-virt
```

On a physical machine with virtualization enabled, the first command prints a number above 0 (one per logical CPU), `lsmod` shows `kvm` plus `kvm_intel` or `kvm_amd`, and `systemd-detect-virt` prints `none`. Inside a cloud VM, `systemd-detect-virt` names the hypervisor instead, for example `kvm`, `amazon` or `microsoft`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Run the commands on your laptop and on a cloud VM. Explain each difference.
2. Why does a guest kernel bug not crash other VMs on the same host?
3. A host has 64 cores and runs VMs with 128 vCPUs in total. What happens when every VM is busy at once?

## References
- [KVM project](https://www.linux-kvm.org/)
- [systemd-detect-virt manual](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-detect-virt.html)

lessons.title: Launch and connect to a cloud VM
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** How virtualization works, basic SSH, and a cloud account with the CLI installed and logged in.

## What you will learn
Which choices you make when you launch a cloud VM, how to reach it safely over SSH, and how to stop paying for it afterwards.

## The choices behind every launch
AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines and Google Compute Engine all ask the same questions:

- **Image:** the disk the VM boots from, for example Debian 12 or Ubuntu 24.04.
- **Machine type:** vCPUs and memory. A Google `e2-small` has 2 shared vCPUs and 2 GB of memory.
- **Region and zone:** where it runs, ideally close to your users.
- **Disk and firewall rules:** storage, and which ports are open.
- **Access:** how you log in. Use SSH keys, never passwords.

VMs are billed while they run, usually per second. A stopped VM costs nothing for compute, but you still pay for its disk until you delete it.

## Access without exposing the VM
Bots find an open port 22 within minutes. Limit SSH to your own IP address at the very least. Google's auto-created `default` network has a rule allowing SSH from anywhere, so check it. Better still, skip public SSH: Google IAP TCP forwarding, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager and Azure Bastion reach a VM without one.

## Worked example
Launch a small Debian VM on Google Cloud, allow SSH only from your address, and connect.

```bash
gcloud compute instances create web-1 \
  --zone=us-central1-a --machine-type=e2-small \
  --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud --tags=web

gcloud compute firewall-rules create ssh-from-me \
  --network=default --allow=tcp:22 \
  --source-ranges=<your-public-ip>/32 --target-tags=web

gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=us-central1-a
```

The first time, `gcloud compute ssh` creates a key pair in `~/.ssh/google_compute_engine` and installs the public key for you. Inside the VM:

```bash
grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release
nproc
free -h
```

You should see `Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)`, `2` CPUs and about 2 GB of total memory. Exit, then delete the VM so it stops billing:

```bash
gcloud compute instances delete web-1 --zone=us-central1-a
```

On AWS the equivalent launch is `aws ec2 run-instances --image-id <ami-id> --instance-type t3.micro --key-name <key-name> --security-group-ids <sg-id>`, and `aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids <instance-id>` removes it.

## Practice and self-review
1. Launch, connect and delete the VM, then confirm with `gcloud compute instances list`.
2. Find the rule in the `default` network that opens port 22 to `0.0.0.0/0`. What would you change?
3. Explain the cost difference between a stopped VM and a deleted VM.
4. Connect with `gcloud compute ssh web-1 --zone=us-central1-a --tunnel-through-iap`. Why can this work without an external IP?

## References
- [Compute Engine documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs)
- [Amazon EC2 documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/)

lessons.title: Images, cloud-init and Packer
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Launch and connect to a cloud VM, and basic YAML. ## What you will learn Why you build VMs from code instead of configuring them by hand, and when to use cloud-init, Packer or Ansible. ## Why hand-built servers fail If you SSH in and install packages by hand, nobody can rebuild that server exactly. Small fixes pile up and servers drift apart. When one dies, or you need ten more, you are guessing. Treat a VM as disposable instead: everything it needs is in code, so each new one is identical. ## Three tools, three jobs - **cloud-init** runs on first boot. It reads a config, called user data, from the cloud's metadata service, then installs packages, writes files and runs commands. Most Linux cloud images, including Ubuntu, ship with it. Its output goes to `/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`. - **Packer** bakes a **golden image**. It starts a temporary VM, runs your install steps, saves the disk as a reusable image and deletes the VM. You run `packer init .` and `packer build .` against a template. - **Ansible** connects over SSH and configures servers that already exist. It needs no agent, so it suits long-lived fleets. The main trade-off is boot time. Installing packages on every boot can take minutes and fails if a package mirror is down. A baked image boots ready to serve. A common pattern: bake the slow, stable parts with Packer, and use cloud-init only for per-instance settings. Terraform, covered in its own topic, then creates the VMs. ## Worked example Save this as `cloud-init.yaml`: ```yaml #cloud-config package_update: true packages: - nginx write_files: - path: /var/www/html/index.html content: |

built by cloud-init

runcmd: - systemctl enable --now nginx ``` The first line must be exactly `#cloud-config`, or cloud-init ignores the file. Test it locally with Multipass, which runs Ubuntu VMs on your laptop: ```bash multipass launch --name web --cloud-init cloud-init.yaml multipass exec web -- cloud-init status --wait multipass exec web -- curl -s localhost multipass delete --purge web ``` `cloud-init status --wait` blocks until first boot finishes, then prints `status: done`. `curl` prints `

built by cloud-init

`. On `status: error`, read the output log inside the VM. In the cloud, pass the same file as user data: `--user-data file://cloud-init.yaml` with `aws ec2 run-instances`, or `--metadata-from-file=user-data=cloud-init.yaml` with `gcloud compute instances create` on an Ubuntu image. ## Practice and self-review 1. Add a `users` entry to the file that creates a user with your SSH public key. Launch again and log in as that user. 2. Your VMs take four minutes to become healthy because cloud-init installs Java. What would you move into a Packer image? 3. When would you choose Ansible over a new image? ## References - [cloud-init documentation](https://cloudinit.readthedocs.io/) - [Packer documentation](https://developer.hashicorp.com/packer/docs)

lessons.title: Scaling VMs and when to choose them
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Images, cloud-init and Packer, and what a load balancer does.

## What you will learn
How groups of identical VMs scale and heal themselves, and when VMs still beat containers.

## Groups built from a template
You write an **instance template** (AWS: launch template) with the image, machine type and startup config. A group keeps a number of identical VMs running from it: AWS Auto Scaling groups, Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Google managed instance groups (MIGs).

A group does three jobs:

- **Autoscaling:** adds VMs when a metric, usually average CPU, rises above a target, and removes them when it falls.
- **Autohealing:** with a health check, replaces VMs that stop answering.
- **Rolling updates:** replaces VMs a few at a time when you change the template.

Scaling in deletes VMs, so each VM must be stateless. Keep sessions and data elsewhere.

## Set targets for slow starts
A new VM must boot, run its startup steps and warm up. That often takes one to three minutes. At a 90% CPU target, users feel the overload long before help arrives. Around 60% leaves headroom, and a baked image shortens the wait. A cool-down period stops the autoscaler from reading metrics of VMs that are still starting.

## When VMs are the right choice
Choose VMs for a custom kernel or kernel modules, legacy software tied to one OS, per-host licensing, GPUs with special drivers, or a hard isolation boundary between tenants. Otherwise containers are usually cheaper and faster to ship. They still run on VMs: Kubernetes nodes are VMs in a group like this.

## Worked example
Create a Google MIG that scales between two and six VMs. Save `startup.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx
```

Then run:

```bash
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-tmpl \
  --machine-type=e2-small --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
  --metadata-from-file=startup-script=startup.sh

gcloud compute instance-groups managed create web-mig \
  --zone=us-central1-a --template=web-tmpl --size=2

gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling web-mig \
  --zone=us-central1-a --min-num-replicas=2 --max-num-replicas=6 \
  --target-cpu-utilization=0.6 --cool-down-period=90

gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances web-mig --zone=us-central1-a
```

You should see two instances named `web-mig-…` with status `RUNNING`. Delete one with `gcloud compute instances delete <instance-name> --zone=us-central1-a`, list again, and watch the group recreate it. Clean up with `gcloud compute instance-groups managed delete web-mig --zone=us-central1-a`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Why does a 90% CPU target hurt users during a traffic spike?
2. Your VMs keep shopping carts in local memory. What breaks when the group scales in?
3. Name two workloads on your team that should stay on VMs, and why.

## References
- [Managed instance groups](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups)
- [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/)

topics.summary: Package applications into portable container images and run them anywhere.

lessons.title: Containers vs VMs
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** How virtualization works (from the Virtual Machines topic) and basic Linux processes. Docker installed.

## What you will learn
What a container really is, why it starts so much faster than a VM, and what you give up in exchange.

## A container is an isolated process
A VM runs a whole guest operating system on virtual hardware. A container does not. It is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel isolates in two ways:

- **Namespaces** change what the process can see. The PID namespace gives it its own process list, the network namespace its own interfaces and ports, and the mount namespace its own filesystem.
- **Cgroups** limit what it can use: CPU time, memory and the number of processes.

There is no guest kernel to boot, so a container starts in well under a second once its image is on disk. Images are often tens of megabytes, not the gigabytes of a VM disk.

An **image** is a read-only stack of filesystem layers plus metadata, such as the command to run. A **container** is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top. Delete the container and that layer is gone, which is why lasting data goes in volumes (see the advanced lesson on networking and volumes).

## What you give up
Every container on a host shares one kernel. A kernel vulnerability can let a process escape to the host, which a VM boundary would usually contain. For untrusted code, teams use sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers, or Firecracker microVMs.

Linux containers also need a Linux kernel. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs them inside a small Linux VM.

## Worked example
```bash
docker run --rm -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
curl -s http://localhost:8080 | grep title
docker top web
docker stop web
```

`curl` prints `<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>`. `docker top` lists the nginx master and worker processes: real processes on the host. `--rm` deletes the container when it stops.

Now look at the isolation:

```bash
docker run --rm alpine ps
docker run --rm alpine uname -r
docker run --rm --memory 64m alpine cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max
```

`ps` shows only itself, as PID 1: the PID namespace hides everything else. `uname -r` prints the same kernel version as `uname -r` on a Linux host (on Docker Desktop, the kernel of its VM). The last command prints `67108864`, the 64 MB limit, on hosts that use cgroup v2.

## Practice and self-review
1. Time `docker run --rm alpine true` with `time`. Compare it with how long a cloud VM takes to boot.
2. Run `docker run --rm --pid=host alpine ps` on a Linux host. What changed, and why is that flag risky?
3. Your platform runs code uploaded by customers. Are plain containers enough? What would you add?

## References
- [Docker get started](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/)
- [Linux namespaces manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html)

lessons.title: Writing a Dockerfile
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Containers vs VMs, and basic Node.js and npm. Docker installed.

## What you will learn
What the common Dockerfile instructions do, and how to order them so rebuilds take seconds, not minutes.

## What each instruction does
A Dockerfile is a recipe for an image, run top to bottom:

- `FROM` picks the base image.
- `WORKDIR` sets, and creates, the working directory.
- `COPY` copies files from the **build context**, the folder you pass to `docker build`.
- `RUN` runs a command at build time and saves the result.
- `ENV` sets an environment variable for later steps and the running container.
- `EXPOSE` only documents the port; `-p` on `docker run` publishes it.
- `USER` switches away from root. Official Node images include a `node` user.
- `CMD` is the default command. Use the JSON (exec) form, `["node", "server.js"]`, so your app is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` on stop. The shell form wraps it in `/bin/sh`, which may not pass the signal on.

## Layer order and the build cache
`RUN`, `COPY` and `ADD` each create a layer. On a rebuild, Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its input files are unchanged. As soon as one layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt.

So copy `package.json` and `package-lock.json` and install dependencies before copying your source. Source changes all day, dependencies rarely, so most rebuilds skip `npm ci`. Put what changes least at the top.

A `.dockerignore` file keeps `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env` out of the build context. Builds get faster, a local `node_modules` cannot overwrite the image's, and secrets stay out of layers. Multi-stage builds, the next lesson, shrink images further.

## Worked example
`server.js`:

```javascript
const http = require("http");
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
http.createServer((req, res) => res.end("hello from a container\n"))
  .listen(port, () => console.log(`listening on ${port}`));
process.on("SIGTERM", () => process.exit(0));
```

Run `npm init -y`, then `npm install` to create `package-lock.json`. Add a `.dockerignore` listing `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env`. Then the `Dockerfile`:

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
ENV PORT=3000
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run --rm -d --name myapp -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0
curl http://localhost:3000
docker stop myapp
```

`curl` prints `hello from a container`. `docker stop` returns quickly because the app handles `SIGTERM`. Now change the message and build again. The `RUN npm ci` step is marked `CACHED`; only the steps from `COPY . .` onward run.

## Practice and self-review
1. Move `COPY . .` above `RUN npm ci`, change `server.js`, and rebuild. What happens to the install step?
2. Change `CMD` to the shell form and time `docker stop`. Explain any difference.
3. Run `docker history myapp:1.0` and match each layer to a Dockerfile line.

## References
- [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/)
- [Docker build cache](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/)

lessons.title: Multi-stage builds and small images
lessons.content:
## Build in one stage, ship in another

Build in one stage, ship only the output:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /app /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

## Why smaller images matter

Smaller images mean faster pulls and a smaller attack surface. Scan with `docker scout` or `trivy`.

lessons.title: Docker Compose for multi-service apps
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Writing a Dockerfile, and running single containers with `docker run`.

## What you will learn
How to describe several containers, their network, volumes and start order in one file, and run the whole stack with one command.

## What Compose gives you
A real app is rarely one container. An API, a database and a cache each need ports, environment variables and volumes, and typing those as `docker run` flags is error-prone. Compose puts it all in `compose.yaml` (`docker-compose.yml` also works), and `docker compose up` starts everything.

Compose also:

- creates a network for the project, where each service reaches the others by its service name, such as `db`;
- creates named volumes that survive `docker compose down`;
- prefixes containers, networks and volumes with the project name, by default the folder name.

Use `docker compose` (Compose v2). The top-level `version:` key is obsolete.

## Start order is not readiness
`depends_on` starts the database container first, but a started container is not a ready database. Postgres needs a few seconds to accept connections, so an API that connects at startup crashes. Add a `healthcheck` to the database and use `condition: service_healthy`, so the dependent service waits until the check passes.

Keep passwords out of the file. Compose reads a `.env` file in the project folder and substitutes `${VARIABLE}` values. Do not commit `.env`.

Compose runs on one host, which suits local development and CI. For many hosts and self-healing, use an orchestrator such as Kubernetes. This project's root `docker-compose.yml` uses Compose to run Postgres, the backend services and the frontend together on your machine.

## Worked example
Save as `compose.yaml`. Adminer, a small database web UI, stands in for your API; in your own project you would write `build: .` instead of `image:`.

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-devpass}
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
  admin:
    image: adminer
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose exec db psql -U postgres -c "select version();"
docker compose down
```

`docker compose ps` shows `db` as `healthy`, and `admin` starts only after that. Open `http://localhost:8080` and log in with server `db`, user `postgres` and password `devpass`. The server name works because both services share the project network. `docker compose down` removes the containers and network but keeps `pgdata`. Add `-v` to delete the volume too.

## Practice and self-review
1. Remove the `healthcheck` and the condition. What does `depends_on` still guarantee?
2. Create a table, run `docker compose down`, then `up -d`. Is the table still there? Repeat with `down -v`.
3. Set `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` in a `.env` file and confirm the new password is used on a fresh volume. Why does it not change an existing one?

## References
- [Docker Compose documentation](https://docs.docker.com/compose/)
- [Compose file reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/)

topics.summary: Orchestrate containers: scheduling, self-healing, scaling and service discovery.

lessons.title: Kubernetes architecture
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Containers vs VMs and Writing a Dockerfile (Docker topic), and basic YAML. Docker, `kubectl` and `kind` installed.

## What you will learn
What runs inside a Kubernetes cluster, what each part does, and how they turn the state you declare into running containers.

## The control plane
The control plane makes decisions for the whole cluster:

- **kube-apiserver** is the front door. `kubectl`, controllers and nodes all talk to it, and it is the only component that reads and writes etcd.
- **etcd** is a consistent key-value store that holds every object. It uses the Raft protocol, so production clusters run three or five members and survive losing one or two.
- **kube-scheduler** picks a node for each new pod, based on its CPU and memory requests, affinity rules and taints.
- **kube-controller-manager** runs control loops: the Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node and Job controllers, among others.

On EKS, AKS or GKE, the provider runs the control plane for you.

## Worker nodes
Each node runs:

- **kubelet**, which watches for pods assigned to its node, asks the container runtime to start them and reports their status;
- a **container runtime**, such as containerd or CRI-O, reached through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). Images built with Docker run unchanged;
- **kube-proxy**, which programs packet rules so Service addresses reach the right pods;
- a **CNI plugin**, which gives every pod its own IP address.

## Desired state and reconciliation
You do not tell Kubernetes to "start three containers". You store desired state, such as "three replicas of this pod", through the API server. Each controller loops: compare desired with actual, act on the difference, repeat. If a node dies, controllers create replacement pods elsewhere. Components do not call each other; they watch the API server and react.

## Worked example
```bash
kind create cluster --name demo
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```

`kind` runs the cluster inside a Docker container. You should see one `Ready` node, `demo-control-plane`. In `kube-system` you will find `etcd-demo-control-plane`, `kube-apiserver-demo-control-plane`, `kube-controller-manager-…`, `kube-scheduler-…`, `kube-proxy-…`, `coredns-…` and `kindnet-…` (kind's CNI plugin). On a managed cluster, the control-plane pods are not visible.

Now watch the chain of components react:

```bash
kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
```

Read the events in order: the deployment controller scales a ReplicaSet, the ReplicaSet controller creates a pod, `default-scheduler` reports `Scheduled`, and the kubelet reports `Pulling`, `Created` and `Started`. Clean up with `kind delete cluster --name demo`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Delete the `hello` pod with `kubectl delete pod -l app=hello`. Which controller brings it back?
2. If the scheduler stops, what happens to pods that are already running? To new ones?
3. Why must etcd be backed up, and why does a three-member etcd survive only one failure?

## References
- [Kubernetes components](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/)
- [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/)

lessons.title: Pods, Deployments and ReplicaSets
lessons.content:
## Declare a deployment

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports: [{ containerPort: 80 }]
```

## Apply it and watch it recover

```bash
kubectl apply -f web.yaml
kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl delete pod -l app=web   # watch them come back
```

lessons.title: Services and Ingress
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Pods, Deployments and ReplicaSets. A local cluster with the `web` Deployment from that lesson (label `app: web`, image `nginx:1.27`).

## What you will learn
How a Service gives a changing set of pods one stable address, which Service type to use, and how an Ingress routes outside HTTP traffic to Services.

## Why pods need a Service
Pods are replaced all the time: during a rollout, after a crash, when a node drains. Each replacement gets a new IP, and clients cannot track that.

A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name: `web` in the same namespace, or `web.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` anywhere in the cluster. It selects pods by label. Kubernetes keeps an **EndpointSlice** of the matching pods that are ready, and kube-proxy spreads connections across them. A pod failing its readiness probe leaves that list and stops getting traffic. `port` is what clients call; `targetPort` is where the container listens.

## Service types
- **ClusterIP** (default): reachable only inside the cluster.
- **NodePort**: also opens a port, 30000 to 32767 by default, on every node.
- **LoadBalancer**: also asks the cloud for an external load balancer, which costs money.
- **Headless** (`clusterIP: None`): no virtual IP; DNS returns pod IPs. StatefulSets use this.

## Ingress routes HTTP by host and path
One load balancer per service gets expensive. An **Ingress** lets one entry point route by host and path, for example `api.example.com` to the `api` Service, and can terminate TLS.

An Ingress does nothing on its own. An **ingress controller** in the cluster, such as Traefik or a cloud provider's controller, reads it and configures a proxy. The Kubernetes project has announced the retirement of the community ingress-nginx controller, so check yours is maintained. For new work, look at the **Gateway API**, which is more expressive and splits duties between platform and app teams.

## Worked example
```bash
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl get service web
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://web
```

You should see type `ClusterIP`, an EndpointSlice with three pod IPs, and the nginx welcome page, found by the DNS name `web`. Then apply this `ingress.yaml` with `kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  rules:
    - host: web.example.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  number: 80
```

`kubectl get ingress web` shows an empty `ADDRESS`: no controller is installed, so nothing acts on the rule.

## Practice and self-review
1. Scale `web` to 5 replicas and check the EndpointSlice again.
2. Change the Service selector to `app: wrong`. What do the endpoints and the `wget` call show?
3. When would you choose NodePort, LoadBalancer or an Ingress?

## References
- [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/)
- [Ingress](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)
- [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/)

lessons.title: ConfigMaps, Secrets and probes
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Pods, Deployments and ReplicaSets, and Services and Ingress.

## What you will learn
How to keep configuration and secrets out of images, and how probes decide whether a pod gets traffic or a restart.

## ConfigMaps and Secrets
Build one image; keep what changes between environments, such as URLs and passwords, outside it. A **ConfigMap** holds non-secret key-value pairs. A **Secret** has the same shape, for sensitive values.

Pods use them as environment variables (`envFrom` or `env`) or mounted files. Environment variables are read at container start, so after changing a ConfigMap, restart the pods: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>`. Mounted files refresh after a short delay.

A Secret is **base64-encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone who can read the object can read the value. Restrict access with RBAC (see the advanced security lesson), enable encryption at rest for etcd, and never commit Secret YAML. In production, the External Secrets Operator syncs them from a cloud secret manager.

## Readiness, liveness and startup probes
The kubelet probes each container:

- **Readiness:** should this pod get traffic? On failure the pod leaves its Service's endpoints. It is not restarted.
- **Liveness:** is this container stuck? On failure the kubelet restarts it.
- **Startup:** holds off the other two until a slow-starting app is up.

By default a probe runs every 10 seconds, times out after 1 second, and acts after 3 failures in a row. Keep liveness simple. If it checks the database, a database outage restarts every pod. Put dependency checks in readiness.

## Worked example
```bash
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=GREETING=hello
kubectl create secret generic app-secrets --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret
kubectl get secret app-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
```

The last command prints `s3cret`: base64 protects nothing. Save as `config-demo.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef: { name: app-config }
        - secretRef: { name: app-secrets }
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: { path: /index.html, port: 80 }
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        tcpSocket: { port: 80 }
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f config-demo.yaml
kubectl exec config-demo -- printenv GREETING
kubectl exec config-demo -- rm /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
kubectl get pod config-demo -w
```

`printenv` prints `hello`. Once the page is gone, readiness gets 404s and within about 15 seconds `READY` shows `0/1`. `RESTARTS` stays 0: liveness only checks that port 80 accepts connections. Restore it with `kubectl exec config-demo -- sh -c 'echo ok > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'` and the pod is ready again.

## Practice and self-review
1. Make liveness an `httpGet` on `/index.html` and repeat. What happens to `RESTARTS`, and why does the page come back?
2. Change `GREETING` in the ConfigMap. Does `printenv` change without a restart?
3. Your service needs 90 seconds to warm a cache. Which probe protects it from liveness?

## References
- [Secrets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/)
- [Liveness, readiness and startup probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)

lessons.title: Autoscaling, Helm and GitOps
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** Pods, Deployments and ReplicaSets, Services and Ingress, and ConfigMaps, Secrets and probes. A local `kind` cluster.

## What you will learn
How the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decides how many replicas to run, and where Helm, Kustomize and GitOps fit when you manage many manifests.

## How the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decides
The **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** (HPA) changes a Deployment's replica count based on a metric. It needs **metrics-server** for CPU and memory. CPU utilization is measured against each pod's CPU **request**, so without requests there is no percentage.

About every 15 seconds it computes:

`desired = ceil(current replicas × current metric / target)`

With 4 replicas at 140% of their request and a 70% target, it asks for 8. Scaling down waits for a 5-minute stabilization window by default, so a short dip does not remove pods you need again.

The HPA only adds pods. If no node has room, they stay `Pending` until a node autoscaler, such as Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, adds nodes. Managed services (EKS, AKS, GKE) run the control plane and offer node autoscaling.

## Helm, Kustomize and GitOps
A real service needs many manifests across several environments. Three tools help; the Helm and GitOps topic teaches each:

- **Helm** packages templated manifests as a **chart** with a `values.yaml`, and keeps release history for `helm rollback`.
- **Kustomize** applies template-free overlays, built into `kubectl apply -k`.
- **Argo CD** and **Flux** (GitOps) keep the cluster matching a Git repository and correct drift.

## Worked example
Install metrics-server. On kind it needs `--kubelet-insecure-tls`, because kubelet certificates there are self-signed.

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
kubectl patch deployment metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl set resources deployment web --requests=cpu=50m
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80
```

Save as `hpa.yaml` and apply it with `kubectl apply -f hpa.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

Generate load, then watch:

```bash
kubectl run load --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  sh -c 'while true; do wget -q -O- http://web > /dev/null; done'
kubectl get hpa web --watch
```

Within a minute or two, `TARGETS` climbs above 70% and `REPLICAS` rises. Run `kubectl delete pod load`. About five minutes later, replicas drop back to 2.

## Practice and self-review
1. Remove the CPU request and check `kubectl describe hpa web`. What error appears?
2. Calculate the desired replicas for 3 pods at 210% with a 70% target. Check it against the formula.
3. Your HPA wants 20 pods but 12 are `Pending`. What is missing?

## References
- [Horizontal Pod Autoscaling](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/)
- [Helm documentation](https://helm.sh/docs/)

lessons.title: Accounts, regions and IAM
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** A terminal, the AWS CLI v2 installed, and access to an AWS account.

## What you will learn
How accounts, regions and availability zones fit together, how IAM decides whether a request is allowed, and how to sign in to the CLI without long-lived keys.

## Accounts, regions and availability zones
An **account** is the boundary for billing, resources and security. Use separate accounts for production and development, grouped with AWS Organizations, to contain mistakes.

A **region**, such as `eu-west-1`, is a geographic area. Each region contains several **availability zones** (AZs): separate data centers with their own power and networking. Most services are regional, and your data stays in the region you choose. IAM is global.

## How IAM decides
Every API call is made by a **principal**: the root user, an IAM user, or a **role**. A role has no password. It is assumed, and AWS STS returns temporary credentials that expire.

Permissions come from JSON **policies**:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>/reports/*"
  }]
}
```

Evaluation follows three rules. Everything is denied by default. A request needs an explicit `Allow`. Any explicit `Deny` wins over every `Allow`.

## Protect the account from day one
- Turn on MFA for the root user, create no access keys for it, and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
- Give people **IAM Identity Center** (SSO) access. They get short-lived credentials for a chosen account and permission set.
- Give workloads roles: an instance profile on EC2, an execution role on Lambda. Leaked access keys are abused quickly.

## Worked example
```bash
aws configure sso
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <profile-name>
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-west-1 \
  --query "AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName" --output text --profile <profile-name>
```

`aws configure sso` asks for your start URL and SSO region, opens a browser to approve, then lets you pick an account, a role and a profile name. `get-caller-identity` needs no permissions and prints your `Account` and an `Arn` such as `arn:aws:sts::<account-id>:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_<permission-set>_<id>/<you>`. The last command prints zone names such as `eu-west-1a eu-west-1b eu-west-1c`. When the session expires, run `aws sso login --profile <profile-name>`. Nothing here creates billable resources.

## Practice and self-review
1. Another policy attached to the same role denies `s3:*` on that bucket. Can the role still read `reports/q1.csv`? Why?
2. Run the AZ command for two other regions and compare the counts.
3. Explain why an EC2 instance should use a role instead of keys in `~/.aws/credentials`.

## References
- [IAM User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html)
- [Policy evaluation logic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html)
- [Configure the CLI with IAM Identity Center](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html)

lessons.title: VPC networking
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Accounts, regions and IAM* lesson, and CIDR notation such as `10.0.0.0/16`.

## What you will learn
How a VPC, its subnets and route tables decide what can reach the internet, and how security groups differ from network ACLs.

## Address space and subnets
A **VPC** is a private network in one region. It spans every AZ in that region. You split its CIDR block into **subnets**. Each subnet lives in exactly one AZ, so use at least two.

AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet: the first four and the last. A `/24` therefore gives you 251 usable addresses, not 256.

## What makes a subnet public
"Public" is not a checkbox. It is the **route table**:

- A **public subnet** has a route `0.0.0.0/0` to an **Internet Gateway**, and its instances need public IP addresses.
- A **private subnet** sends `0.0.0.0/0` to a **NAT Gateway** placed in a public subnet. Instances can connect out, but nothing can connect in.

A NAT Gateway is zonal and billed per hour and per GB processed. It is a common surprise cost. Free gateway endpoints keep S3 and DynamoDB traffic off it.

## Security groups and network ACLs
A **security group** is attached to a network interface. It is stateful, so return traffic is allowed automatically. It has allow rules only. A new group denies all inbound and allows all outbound. A rule can name another group as its source: "the database group allows port 5432 from the app group".

A **network ACL** applies to a whole subnet. It is stateless, with numbered allow and deny rules checked lowest first, so return traffic on ephemeral ports (1024-65535) needs its own rule. Most teams leave the default NACL, which allows everything.

## Worked example
```bash
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 \
  --availability-zone <az-name> --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids "$SUBNET_ID" \
  --query "Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount"
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values="$VPC_ID" \
  --query "RouteTables[].Routes[]"
```

You should see `251`, then a single route: `10.0.0.0/16` to `local`. With no route to the internet, this subnet is private. VPCs and subnets cost nothing. Clean up with `aws ec2 delete-subnet --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID"`, then `aws ec2 delete-vpc --vpc-id "$VPC_ID"`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Plan public and private subnets in three AZs inside a `/16`.
2. A NACL allows inbound TCP 443, yet HTTPS clients time out. Why?
3. Why is "allow 5432 from the app security group" better than "allow 5432 from 10.0.0.0/16"?

## References
- [Amazon VPC User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/what-is-amazon-vpc.html)
- [NAT gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html)

lessons.title: Compute and storage
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Accounts, regions and IAM* and *VPC networking* lessons.

## What you will learn
How to choose between EC2, Lambda, ECS on Fargate and EKS, how S3, EBS and EFS differ, and how to work with S3 from the command line.

## Choosing compute
Start with the most managed option that fits, and move down only when you need control:

- **Lambda** runs a function per event. You pay per request and per millisecond of run time. One invocation can run for at most 15 minutes. The *Serverless* lesson goes deeper.
- **ECS on Fargate** runs containers without servers to manage. You pay for the vCPU and memory each task requests.
- **EKS** gives you the Kubernetes API. It adds an hourly charge per cluster, and you still own upgrades and add-ons.
- **EC2** is a virtual machine. You patch the OS. Linux instances are billed per second while running.

## Block, file and object storage
- **EBS** is a block volume, like a disk, attached to one instance. It lives in one AZ and survives a stop. A root volume is deleted on terminate by default. Snapshots back it up.
- **EFS** is a shared NFS file system. Many instances in several AZs mount it at once, and you pay for the GB stored.
- **S3** stores objects in buckets over an HTTPS API. It is not a file system: `notes/` is a key prefix, not a folder. Bucket names are globally unique. Reads after writes are strongly consistent. New buckets block public access and encrypt objects by default.

## Worked example
```bash
BUCKET=<unique-bucket-name>
aws s3 mb "s3://$BUCKET" --region <region>
echo "hello from s3" > hello.txt
aws s3 cp hello.txt "s3://$BUCKET/notes/hello.txt"
aws s3 ls "s3://$BUCKET" --recursive
aws s3 presign "s3://$BUCKET/notes/hello.txt" --expires-in 300
```

You should see `make_bucket: <unique-bucket-name>`, an `upload:` line, and a listing that shows `14` bytes for `notes/hello.txt`. `presign` prints a URL that anyone can use for five minutes. Run `curl "<url>"` and you get `hello from s3`. After it expires, S3 returns an error instead.

A few small objects cost a fraction of a cent. Clean up with `aws s3 rb "s3://$BUCKET" --force`, which deletes the objects and then the bucket.

## Practice and self-review
1. Pick storage for each: PostgreSQL data files on one EC2 instance; uploads shared by four web servers that expect a POSIX path; user avatars served to browsers.
2. A nightly job takes 40 minutes. Why is Lambda a poor fit, and what would you use?
3. You stop an EC2 instance for a week. What do you still pay for?

## References
- [Amazon EC2 documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ec2/)
- [Amazon S3 User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html)
- [AWS CLI s3 commands](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3/)

lessons.title: Databases, monitoring and cost
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *VPC networking* and *Compute and storage* lessons.

## What you will learn
How to choose a managed database, and how CloudWatch, CloudTrail and billing tools show what your system does, who changed it, and what it costs.

## Managed databases
- **RDS** runs PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server or Db2. AWS patches the engine and takes automated backups, kept 1 to 35 days, so you can restore to any second in that window. **Multi-AZ** keeps a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically, typically in one to two minutes.
- **Aurora** is MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible. It keeps six copies of your data across three AZs.
- **DynamoDB** is a key-value and document store. You design keys around your access patterns.
- **ElastiCache** is an in-memory cache (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached).

Place databases in private subnets, reachable only from the app's security group. Multi-AZ protects you from an AZ failure, not from a bad `DELETE`. Backups do that.

## Observe with CloudWatch and CloudTrail
**CloudWatch** collects metrics, logs and alarms. EC2 sends CPU and network metrics every five minutes by default. Memory and disk usage need the CloudWatch agent. Log groups keep data forever unless you set a retention period. Alarms notify an SNS topic.

**CloudTrail** records API calls: who did what, from where, and when. Event history shows the last 90 days of management events at no cost. Create a trail to keep them longer in S3.

## Watch the bill
Cost Explorer shows spend by service and tag. Budgets alert you before a limit is reached; the *Well-Architected* lesson creates one. Common surprises are NAT Gateways, idle RDS instances, unattached EBS volumes and log storage.

## Worked example
```bash
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=CreateVpc \
  --max-results 5 \
  --query "Events[].[EventTime,Username,EventName]" --output table
aws logs create-log-group --log-group-name /lesson/demo
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /lesson/demo --retention-in-days 7
aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /lesson/demo \
  --query "logGroups[].[logGroupName,retentionInDays]" --output text
```

If you ran the VPC lesson's example in this region, the table shows that `CreateVpc` call and the identity that made it. Otherwise try `RunInstances`. The last command prints `/lesson/demo	7`. An empty log group costs nothing. Remove it with `aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /lesson/demo`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Choose a database: orders with joins and transactions; a session store with expiry; profile lookups by ID at very high volume.
2. Create an alarm for EC2 `CPUUtilization` above 80% for three 5-minute periods.
3. Someone stopped a production instance last night. Find out who, using only CloudTrail.

## References
- [Amazon RDS User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html)
- [Amazon CloudWatch User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch.html)
- [AWS CloudTrail User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide.html)

lessons.title: Resource hierarchy and Entra ID
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** A terminal, the Azure CLI installed, and an Azure subscription where you are Owner.

## What you will learn
How management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources nest, how Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC grant access, and why apps should use managed identities.

## Four levels of scope
Azure organizes everything as: **management groups** > **subscriptions** > **resource groups** > **resources**.

- A **subscription** is a billing and quota boundary. It trusts exactly one Entra tenant. Teams use separate subscriptions for production and development.
- A **resource group** holds related resources that share a lifecycle. Every resource belongs to exactly one group. The group has a location for its metadata, but its resources can be in other regions.
- Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it. That makes cleanup easy and mistakes expensive.

## Entra ID and Azure RBAC
**Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD) is the identity service.

Access to resources uses **Azure RBAC**. A **role assignment** has three parts: a principal, a role and a scope. It applies to that scope and everything below it, and assignments add up. Common built-in roles:

- **Reader**: view everything, change nothing.
- **Contributor**: create and manage resources, but not grant access.
- **Owner**: everything, including role assignments.
- Data roles such as **Storage Blob Data Reader** control the data inside a service.

Entra roles, such as Global Administrator, manage the directory. They are separate from Azure RBAC roles, which manage resources.

## Managed identities instead of secrets
A **managed identity** is an Entra identity that Azure creates for a resource. Your code asks the platform for a token, so there is no secret to store or rotate. A **system-assigned** identity is deleted with its resource. A **user-assigned** identity is a standalone resource that several apps can share.

## Worked example
```bash
az login
az group create --name rg-lesson --location eastus
az identity create --resource-group rg-lesson --name id-lesson
PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az identity show -g rg-lesson -n id-lesson --query principalId -o tsv)
RG_ID=$(az group show -n rg-lesson --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role Reader --scope "$RG_ID"
az role assignment list --scope "$RG_ID" --query "[].roleDefinitionName" -o tsv
```

You should see `Reader` in the list. Resource groups and managed identities are free. Keep `rg-lesson` for the next lessons, or delete it with `az group delete --name rg-lesson --yes`.

## Practice and self-review
1. The identity has Reader on `rg-lesson`. What changes if you assign it at the subscription instead?
2. Why should a CI pipeline get Contributor on one resource group rather than Owner on the subscription?
3. Explain the difference between a Global Administrator and a subscription Owner.

## References
- [Azure Resource Manager overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/overview)
- [What is Azure RBAC?](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/role-based-access-control/overview)
- [Managed identities for Azure resources](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview)

lessons.title: VNets and network security
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Resource hierarchy and Entra ID* lesson, and CIDR notation.

## What you will learn
How to lay out a VNet, how NSG rules are evaluated, and how to reach platform services privately.

## Virtual networks and subnets
A **virtual network** (VNet) is a private network in one region. Unlike AWS, an Azure subnet is regional: it spans all availability zones in the region. Azure reserves five addresses per subnet, so a `/24` gives 251 usable addresses.

Do not rely on implicit outbound internet access for VMs; Microsoft is retiring it. Use a **NAT gateway** for outbound traffic.

## Network security groups
A **network security group** (NSG) attaches to a subnet, a network interface, or both. With both, traffic must pass both. Rules have a priority from 100 to 4096. Lower numbers are checked first, and the first match wins. NSGs are stateful, so replies to allowed traffic pass.

Default rules at priorities 65000 and above allow traffic within the VNet and from the Azure load balancer, allow outbound internet, and deny other inbound traffic. **Service tags** such as `Internet` stand in for IP ranges.

## Private endpoints and load balancing
A **private endpoint** gives one PaaS resource, such as a storage account, a private IP in your subnet. You also need a private DNS zone, such as `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net`, so the usual name resolves to that private IP. Then turn off public network access.

For load balancing: **Load Balancer** handles TCP and UDP in one region, **Application Gateway** handles HTTP in one region with an optional web application firewall, and **Front Door** is a global HTTP entry point.

## Worked example
```bash
az group create --name rg-lesson --location eastus
az network vnet create -g rg-lesson -n vnet-lesson --address-prefixes 10.1.0.0/16 \
  --subnet-name snet-app --subnet-prefixes 10.1.1.0/24
az network nsg create -g rg-lesson -n nsg-app
az network nsg rule create -g rg-lesson --nsg-name nsg-app -n allow-https \
  --priority 200 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes Internet --destination-port-ranges 443
az network vnet subnet update -g rg-lesson --vnet-name vnet-lesson -n snet-app \
  --network-security-group nsg-app
az network nsg rule list -g rg-lesson --nsg-name nsg-app --include-default -o table
```

The table shows `allow-https` at priority 200 and six default rules. VNets and NSGs are free. Clean up with `az group delete --name rg-lesson --yes`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Add a rule at priority 100 that denies 443 from one IP. Which wins, and why?
2. A VM still resolves a storage account with a private endpoint to a public IP. What is missing?
3. Pick a load balancer for a global web app, and for internal TCP traffic.

## References
- [Azure Virtual Network overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-overview)
- [Network security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview)

lessons.title: Compute and containers
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Resource hierarchy and Entra ID* and *VNets and network security* lessons, plus Docker and `kubectl` basics.

## What you will learn
How to choose between VMs, App Service, Functions, Container Apps and AKS, how they pull images, and how to run a container on Container Apps.

## The compute ladder
Each step down gives you more control and more work:

- **Functions** run code per event (see the *Azure Functions* lesson).
- **App Service** hosts web apps from code or a container. You pay for its plan even with no traffic.
- **Container Apps** runs containers on a managed platform with HTTP and event-based autoscaling. It can scale to zero and keeps each deployment as a **revision** you can split traffic between.
- **AKS** gives you the full Kubernetes API. Azure runs the control plane; you own node pools, upgrades and cluster add-ons.
- **Virtual Machines** and **VM Scale Sets** give you the OS to patch.

A sensible default for a new web service is Container Apps. Move to AKS when you need Kubernetes features, operators or custom networking.

## Images and pulling them safely
**Azure Container Registry** (ACR) stores images. Do not turn on the registry's admin user. Give the cluster or app a managed identity with the `AcrPull` role on the registry. For AKS, `az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --attach-acr <registry-name>` sets that up. To use `kubectl` against an existing cluster:

```bash
az aks get-credentials -g <rg> -n <cluster>
kubectl get nodes
```

Each node should show `Ready`.

## Worked example
Deploy Microsoft's sample image to Container Apps:

```bash
az group create --name rg-lesson --location eastus
az provider register --namespace Microsoft.App
az provider register --namespace Microsoft.OperationalInsights
az containerapp up --name ca-hello --resource-group rg-lesson --location eastus \
  --environment env-lesson --image mcr.microsoft.com/k8se/quickstart:latest \
  --target-port 80 --ingress external \
  --query properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn
curl -s "https://<fqdn>" | head -n 5
az containerapp revision list -n ca-hello -g rg-lesson --query "[].name" -o tsv
```

The CLI may offer to install the `containerapp` extension. Creating the environment takes a few minutes. The `up` command prints an address such as `ca-hello.<id>.eastus.azurecontainerapps.io`. `curl` returns the start of an HTML welcome page, and the revision list shows one revision.

The consumption plan has a monthly free grant; the Log Analytics workspace that `up` creates bills for ingested logs. Delete it all with `az group delete --name rg-lesson --yes`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Run `az containerapp update -n ca-hello -g rg-lesson --min-replicas 1`. What does it change for latency and cost?
2. Pick a service: a two-minute nightly script; a team that already ships Helm charts; a legacy Windows app.
3. Why is `AcrPull` through a managed identity safer than the registry admin password?

## References
- [Azure Container Apps overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/overview)
- [Azure Kubernetes Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/)

lessons.title: Data services and monitoring
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Resource hierarchy and Entra ID* and *VNets and network security* lessons.

## What you will learn
How to choose between PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB and Blob Storage, and how Azure Monitor, Log Analytics and Application Insights fit together.

## Data services
- **Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server** is managed PostgreSQL. Backups are kept 7 to 35 days with point-in-time restore. Zone-redundant high availability keeps a standby in another zone. Reach it privately through a VNet or private endpoint.
- **Cosmos DB** is a distributed NoSQL database with several APIs, including NoSQL and MongoDB. It offers five consistency levels, from strong to eventual; session is the default. You pay in request units (RUs), so the partition key decides both speed and cost.
- **Blob Storage** lives in a storage account. Access tiers (hot, cool, cold, archive) trade storage price against read price. Redundancy options include LRS (three copies in one data center) and ZRS (across zones).

## Azure Monitor, Log Analytics and Application Insights
Under **Azure Monitor**:

- **Platform metrics** arrive for most resources automatically.
- The **activity log** records control-plane operations, such as who created or deleted a resource, for 90 days.
- **Resource logs**, such as database query logs, are not stored until you add a **diagnostic setting** that sends them to a **Log Analytics workspace**. You query workspaces with KQL.
- **Application Insights** traces requests, dependencies and exceptions in your app.

Alerts fire on metrics or log queries and notify an **action group**.

## Worked example
Upload a blob with your Entra identity instead of an account key:

```bash
SA=<storage-account-name>
az group create --name rg-lesson --location eastus
az storage account create -g rg-lesson -n "$SA" -l eastus --sku Standard_LRS
az role assignment create --assignee "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \
  --scope "$(az storage account show -g rg-lesson -n "$SA" --query id -o tsv)"
az storage container create --account-name "$SA" -n notes --auth-mode login
echo "hello from blob" > hello.txt
az storage blob upload --account-name "$SA" -c notes -n hello.txt -f hello.txt --auth-mode login
az monitor activity-log list -g rg-lesson --offset 1h \
  --query "[].operationName.localizedValue" -o tsv
```

The name must be 3-24 lowercase letters and digits, globally unique. Owning the subscription does not let you read data, so you assign a data role. It can take a few minutes to apply, so retry on `AuthorizationPermissionMismatch`. The activity log then lists your create operations. Cost is a fraction of a cent. Clean up with `az group delete --name rg-lesson --yes`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Your PostgreSQL slow-query logs never appear in Log Analytics. What did you forget?
2. Orders are read mostly by customer. Why is `customerId` a better Cosmos DB partition key than `country`?

## References
- [Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/overview)
- [Azure Monitor overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/overview)

topics.summary: Projects, IAM, VPC, GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL and BigQuery.

lessons.title: Projects and IAM
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** A terminal, the gcloud CLI installed, and a Google Cloud project with billing enabled.

## What you will learn
How organizations, folders and projects nest, how IAM allow policies bind principals to roles, and why workloads should use service accounts without key files.

## The resource hierarchy
Google Cloud organizes resources as: **organization** > **folders** > **projects** > **resources**.

A **project** is where resources live, APIs are enabled and billing is attached. It has three identifiers: a display name you can change, a **project ID** that is globally unique and permanent, and a numeric **project number**. Deleting a project stops everything in it. You can restore it within 30 days.

## IAM: principals, roles and allow policies
Every resource can have an **allow policy**: a list of bindings, each granting one **role** to some **principals**. Principals look like `user:ana@example.com`, `group:devs@example.com` or `serviceAccount:<name>@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`.

A policy set on a folder is inherited by every project and resource below it. A child cannot take away a role granted higher up. Separate deny policies exist for that.

There are three kinds of role:

- **Basic** roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) cover nearly every service. They are too broad for production.
- **Predefined** roles, such as `roles/storage.objectViewer`, cover one job in one service.
- **Custom** roles list exact permissions when no predefined role fits.

## Service accounts
A **service account** is an identity for a workload. Attach one to a VM or Cloud Run service, and the client libraries find its credentials automatically through **Application Default Credentials**. On your laptop, `gcloud auth application-default login` plays the same role.

Avoid downloaded key files. They are long-lived secrets, and many organizations block them. On GKE, use Workload Identity Federation for GKE instead.

## Worked example
```bash
gcloud init
gcloud config set project <project-id>
gcloud iam service-accounts create lesson-reader --display-name="Lesson reader"
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <project-id> \
  --member="serviceAccount:lesson-reader@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"
gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project-id> \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" \
  --filter="bindings.members:lesson-reader" \
  --format="table(bindings.role)"
```

The last command prints `ROLE` and `roles/storage.objectViewer`. If the project already has conditional bindings, the CLI asks about a condition; add `--condition=None`. Service accounts and IAM are free. Clean up with `gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding` using the same member and role, then `gcloud iam service-accounts delete lesson-reader@<project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Grant the same role on a folder instead. Which projects does it reach?
2. Find a predefined role that can deploy Cloud Run services but not change IAM.
3. Explain why `roles/editor` on a CI service account is risky.

## References
- [IAM overview](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/overview)
- [Resource hierarchy](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/cloud-platform-resource-hierarchy)
- [Service accounts overview](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-overview)

lessons.title: Global VPC networking
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Projects and IAM* lesson, and CIDR notation.

## What you will learn
How a global VPC works, how firewall rules pick targets, and how private VMs reach the internet and managed services.

## A global network with regional subnets
On Google Cloud, a **VPC network** is global. Its **subnets** are regional, and each spans every zone in its region. VMs in `us-central1` and `europe-west1` on the same network talk over internal IPs.

A network is **auto mode**, with a subnet in every region, or **custom mode**, where you create each subnet. New projects often get an auto-mode network called `default`. Use custom mode for real work. Google reserves four addresses in each subnet's primary range, so a `/24` gives 252 usable addresses.

## Firewall rules
VPC firewall rules belong to the network, not to a subnet. Each rule picks its **targets**: all instances, instances with a **network tag**, or instances running as a **service account**. Rules are stateful and have a priority from 0 to 65535; the lower number wins.

Every network has two implied rules at the lowest priority: deny all ingress and allow all egress. You cannot delete them. The `default` network adds broad allow rules; review them.

Prefer service-account targets for sensitive rules. Anyone who can edit a VM can change its tags.

## Outbound access and private services
- **Cloud NAT**, configured on a Cloud Router, gives VMs without external IPs outbound access. Nothing can connect in through it. It is billed per hour and per GB.
- **Private Google Access**, set per subnet, lets those VMs reach Google APIs.
- **Private Service Access** reserves an IP range and peers it with Google's network, so Cloud SQL can have a private IP in your VPC.

## Worked example
```bash
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com
gcloud compute networks create lesson-vpc --subnet-mode=custom
gcloud compute networks subnets create lesson-subnet --network=lesson-vpc \
  --region=us-central1 --range=10.10.0.0/24 --enable-private-ip-google-access
gcloud compute firewall-rules create lesson-allow-iap-ssh --network=lesson-vpc \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=allow --rules=tcp:22 \
  --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=ssh
gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="network:lesson-vpc" \
  --format="table(name,direction,priority,sourceRanges.list())"
```

The list shows one rule at the default priority, 1000, allowing SSH only from Identity-Aware Proxy's range. The implied rules are not listed. Networks, subnets and firewall rules are free. Clean up in reverse order with `gcloud compute firewall-rules delete`, `gcloud compute networks subnets delete` and `gcloud compute networks delete`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Add a second subnet in `europe-west1` on the same network. What routing did you have to set up?
2. A VM with no external IP cannot run `apt-get update`. Which service fixes it, and which does not?

## References
- [VPC overview](https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/overview)
- [VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls)

lessons.title: Compute Engine, Cloud Run and GKE
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Projects and IAM* and *Global VPC networking* lessons, plus Docker basics.

## What you will learn
How to choose between Compute Engine, Cloud Run and GKE, and how to deploy to Cloud Run.

## Compute Engine
**Compute Engine** gives you virtual machines. You pick the machine type, image and zone, and patch the OS. VMs are billed per second, with a one-minute minimum. **Spot VMs** cost much less but can be stopped at any time, so use them for batch work that can retry. A **managed instance group** creates identical VMs from a template, replaces unhealthy ones and scales on load.

## Cloud Run
**Cloud Run** runs a container image and gives it an HTTPS URL. Your container must listen on the port in the `PORT` environment variable, which defaults to 8080. Each deployment creates an immutable **revision**, and you can split traffic between revisions.

One instance handles up to 80 concurrent requests by default. With the default of zero minimum instances, an idle service scales to zero and costs nothing, but the next request waits for a cold start. Set a minimum instance count when latency matters more than cost. **Cloud Run jobs** run containers to completion, for batch tasks.

## GKE
**GKE** gives you the Kubernetes API. It has two modes:

- **Autopilot**: Google manages the nodes, and you pay for the CPU and memory your pods request. Start here.
- **Standard**: you manage node pools, machine types and upgrades, and pay for the nodes.

Both add a cluster management fee. Pick GKE when you need Kubernetes itself: operators, Helm charts, many cooperating services, or portability. A single stateless web service is usually simpler on Cloud Run.

## Worked example
```bash
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com
gcloud run deploy hello \
  --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/cloudrun/container/hello \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --allow-unauthenticated
URL=$(gcloud run services describe hello --region=us-central1 --format="value(status.url)")
curl -s "$URL" | head -n 5
gcloud run revisions list --service=hello --region=us-central1
```

The deploy command prints a `Service URL` ending in `run.app`. `curl` returns the start of an HTML page from Google's sample container, and the revisions list shows one revision serving all traffic. If your organization blocks public services, deploy without `--allow-unauthenticated` and send a token from `gcloud auth print-identity-token`.

A few requests fit within Cloud Run's free tier. Clean up with `gcloud run services delete hello --region=us-central1`.

## Practice and self-review
1. Redeploy with `--min-instances=1`. Time the first request after ten idle minutes, before and after.
2. Pick a service: a 3-hour video encode that can restart; a REST API with spiky traffic; a platform team running twenty services with Helm.
3. Your container listens on port 3000 and the deploy fails its health check. Give two fixes.

## References
- [Cloud Run documentation](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs)
- [Compute Engine documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs)

lessons.title: Data and AI services
lessons.content:
**Prerequisites:** The *Projects and IAM* and *Global VPC networking* lessons.

## What you will learn
How to choose between Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore and Cloud Storage, where BigQuery fits, and how to call a Gemini model through Vertex AI.

## Operational databases
- **Cloud SQL** runs managed PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server. The high-availability setting keeps a standby in another zone of the same region and fails over automatically. Give it a private IP through Private Service Access, and connect with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or IAM database authentication.
- **AlloyDB** is PostgreSQL-compatible, for heavier workloads.
- **Spanner** is a relational database that scales horizontally with strong consistency, across regions if needed. Choose it when one database server is no longer enough, not by default.
- **Firestore** is a serverless document database with real-time listeners, common in web and mobile apps.
- **Memorystore** provides managed Valkey or Redis for caching.

## Storage and analytics
**Cloud Storage** holds objects in buckets. Its classes are Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive. The colder classes have minimum storage durations of 30, 90 and 365 days, and charge more to read.

**BigQuery** is a serverless data warehouse. You query with SQL and pay per data scanned or for reserved capacity. The *BigQuery hands-on* lesson covers it.

## Vertex AI
**Vertex AI** is the platform for machine learning. Use it to call Google models such as Gemini, pick open models from **Model Garden**, train and deploy your own models, and evaluate results. Requests are authorized with IAM, for example `roles/aiplatform.user`. You choose a location, which keeps processing where your data rules require. Model names change often, so check the current list before you pick one.

## Worked example
```bash
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com
PROJECT=<project-id>
MODEL=<gemini-model-id>
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT/locations/us-central1/publishers/google/models/$MODEL:generateContent" \
  -d '{"contents":[{"role":"user","parts":[{"text":"Explain a database index in one sentence."}]}]}'
```

The response is JSON. Your answer is in `candidates[0].content.parts[0].text`, and `usageMetadata` shows the input and output token counts you are billed for. Re-run it and the wording will usually differ. A single short request costs a fraction of a cent. Nothing persistent is created.

## Practice and self-review
1. Choose a store: a product catalog for a mobile app with offline sync; an orders database for one region; a ledger that must accept writes in three continents.
2. You keep yearly audit exports and read them almost never. Which storage class, and what happens if you delete one after a month?
3. Send the same prompt with a `generationConfig` that sets `temperature` to 0. What changes?

## References
- [Cloud SQL documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs)
- [Cloud Storage classes](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)
- [Vertex AI documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs)
